Who I am

I am a web developer, content writer and translator based in North Okkalapa, Yangon. I started with civil engineering studies at Hmaw Bi Technology University, moved into NGO logistics, then into e-commerce operations — and along the way I kept building software for the teams I worked in.

Today I ship websites and content systems for clients abroad while running operations for a Burmese e-commerce brand. I write code, I write copy, and I translate between English and Burmese when a project needs both.

I spent my first years at Hmaw Bi Technology University studying civil engineering — three years of surveying, structures and concrete. Then, like a lot of people in Myanmar, I changed lanes: a B.A. in English, a software development course at KMD Institute, and my first real job in humanitarian logistics at C.D.A.

Those years taught me how supply chains actually behave when the road closes and the deadline does not move. In 2024 I joined NPT Group as a warehouse supervisor, then 321 Ecolife as an operation assistant supervisor — where the job stopped being only boxes and became content, numbers and people.

Why the numbers matter to me

At 321 Ecolife I inherited a TikTok account that was posting without a plan. Over three measured periods we took it from 157,000 to 298,104 followers — a +89.9% jump — with a calendar, a script format and a reporting routine the team could run without me. I like that kind of work: find the lever, build the system, show the graph.

In parallel I have been freelancing as a web developer for clients abroad — Yumeyuki.info, TTS-AE.com and Writermorphosis.com among them — and I still write scripts and translate when a project needs a voice, not just a build.

Now

These days I split my time between running operations for a Burmese e-commerce brand and shipping software for remote clients. The through-line has always been the same: turn messy work into something measurable — a shelf map, a posting calendar, a booking flow, a translation that reads like it was written in the target language.

When I am not working you will find me reading about logistics systems, experimenting with small web tools, or walking around North Okkalapa with a camera.

'content' => '[bs-grid type="portfolio" order="ASC" orderby="menu_order" posts="-1" categories="false" tags="false"]', 'excerpt' => 'Websites, content and systems built for real clients.', ), ); $page_ids = array(); foreach ($kmt_pages as $p) { $existing = get_page_by_path($p['slug']); if ($existing) { $id = $existing->ID; wp_update_post(array( 'ID' => $id, 'post_title' => $p['title'], 'post_content' => $p['content'], 'post_excerpt' => $p['excerpt'], 'post_status' => 'publish', )); } else { $id = wp_insert_post(array( 'post_name' => $p['slug'], 'post_title' => $p['title'], 'post_content' => $p['content'], 'post_excerpt' => $p['excerpt'], 'post_status' => 'publish', 'post_type' => 'page', )); } if ($id && !is_wp_error($id)) { update_post_meta($id, '_wp_page_template', $p['template']); $page_ids[$p['slug']] = (int) $id; } } // --------------------------------------------------------------------------- // Categories + posts // --------------------------------------------------------------------------- $kmt_cats = array( 'Operations' => 'Operations, teams and the systems behind them.', 'Web Development' => 'Building sites, tools and content platforms.', 'Writing' => 'Scripts, copy and translation notes.', 'Warehouse' => 'Shelf maps, pick lists and fulfilment flow.', ); $cat_ids = array(); foreach ($kmt_cats as $name => $desc) { $term = get_term_by('name', $name, 'category'); if (!$term) { $term = wp_insert_term($name, 'category', array('description' => $desc)); } if (!is_wp_error($term)) { $cat_ids[$name] = (int) (is_array($term) ? $term['term_id'] : $term->term_id); } } $kmt_posts = array( array( 'title' => 'Rebuilding a TikTok account from 157K to 298K', 'cat' => 'Operations', 'excerpt' => 'Three periods, one calendar, and +89.9% growth. What the posting routine at 321 Ecolife actually looked like week to week.', 'content' => '

In November 2024 the branch account at 321 Ecolife was 157,000 followers and posting without a plan. By February 2025 it was 298,104 — a jump of +89.9% across three measured periods.

What actually changed

Nothing exotic. Three things, done every week:

  1. A calendar with slots, not ideas. Every slot had a format: product demo, live-session recap, behind-the-shelf clip, community reply.
  2. Scripts before shooting. Fifteen lines, one hook, one proof point, one call to action — written in Burmese first, checked against the English brief.
  3. A Monday number review. Views, saves, follows, and one decision for the week. If a format missed twice, it was cut.

The part nobody photographs

The growth graph is the easy story. The hard story is training two junior operators to keep the routine running on the days I was not there — and making the spreadsheet simple enough that they wanted to use it.

', ), array( 'title' => 'Shelf mapping: cutting pick time with nothing but a diagram', 'cat' => 'Warehouse', 'excerpt' => 'A four-month build at NPT Group turned shelf chaos into a map, a pick list and roughly 25% faster picks.', 'content' => '

When I joined NPT Group as warehouse supervisor, pick time was measured in shrugs. Nobody knew which aisle held what; the experienced staff carried the map in their heads, and every new hire spent weeks rebuilding it.

The intervention

We drew the warehouse. Zone letters, bay numbers, shelf levels — A-03-C meant aisle A, bay 03, level C. Then pick lists were reissued in that order, so a picker walked one loop instead of three.

The map was tape and printed labels. The software came later — but the map came first, and it did most of the work.

Result

Average pick time dropped by roughly a quarter within two months. More importantly, a new operator could pick accurately on day two instead of week three.

', ), array( 'title' => 'Building Writermorphosis: a content platform for writers', 'cat' => 'Web Development', 'excerpt' => 'Custom post types, editorial workflow and front-end filters — how a writer platform gets shaped around submissions.', 'content' => '

Writermorphosis.com needed more than a blog. Writers submit, editors review, and readers browse by form and theme — so the content model had to carry workflow, not just text.

Decisions that mattered

  • Custom post types for submissions versus published pieces, so the editorial queue never leaks into the public feed.
  • Front-end filters by form and theme — readers arrive from social, they will not use a sidebar taxonomy widget.
  • A quiet design: typography does the work, because the product is reading.

The stack is WordPress with a custom theme — the same foundation this site runs on.

', ), array( 'title' => 'From spreadsheets to POS: a four-month car-parts build', 'cat' => 'Web Development', 'excerpt' => 'CSM shelf-mapping and point-of-sale — designing software for staff who did not ask for software.', 'content' => '

The brief was a shelf map and a checkout flow for a car-parts retail operation. The real brief was: stop losing parts in the aisle.

Designing for the floor

Staff did not want an app; they wanted their afternoon back. So every screen started from the physical motion: scan the shelf label, see the bin, tap the part, take the money. Keyboard-first, big targets, no nested menus.

Four months later

The system went live with live stock counts, a pick flow that matches the shelf map, and a POS screen that prints what the counter needs. Adoption was the metric that mattered — and it stuck because the floor team had shaped every screen.

', ), array( 'title' => 'Writing scripts for Canal+ Kids: notes from Program.base', 'cat' => 'Writing', 'excerpt' => 'Two years writing for Program.base, including scripts for Alice Adventure — and what bilingual scripting teaches you.', 'content' => '

Between 2021 and 2022 I wrote for Program.base, including scripts for Canal+ Kids’ Alice Adventure.

What scriptwriting taught me about web work

A script is a user interface for a voice actor: every line is a constraint on timing, pronunciation and energy. Building web pages is the same discipline — every word on a screen is a constraint on someone’s attention.

Translation work (Texas insurance documentation, 2022–2023) sharpened the other muscle: precision under boring conditions. Insurance language does not forgive a soft paraphrase.

', ), array( 'title' => 'Logistics during crisis: lessons from C.D.A', 'cat' => 'Operations', 'excerpt' => 'Procurement, distribution and donor-ready paperwork at an NGO — where a late truck is not a KPI, it is a village.', 'content' => '

At C.D.A (2021–2022) I coordinated procurement and field distribution across Yangon Region. The paperwork discipline there was absolute: every shipment, every vendor, every discrepancy — documented for donors who would read it months later.

Three habits I still use

  1. Write it down while it happens. Memory is a terrible log book.
  2. One source of truth. A stock count in two spreadsheets is two stock counts.
  3. Brief the team before the truck arrives. Most logistics failures are communication failures with a vehicle attached.

', ), array( 'title' => 'TTS-AE.com', 'kicker' => 'Web development · Client', 'excerpt' => 'Corporate site with a bilingual content structure — English and Burmese sharing one navigation.', 'quote' => 'Two languages, one sitemap — the hard part is editorial, not technical.', 'content' => '

Language pairs live as parallel content with shared slugs; the theme renders the switcher inline and keeps SEO metadata correct per language.

', ), array( 'title' => 'Writermorphosis.com', 'kicker' => 'Web development · Client', 'excerpt' => 'Content platform for writers: submissions, editorial workflow and a reader-facing filter layer.', 'quote' => 'Built so the editor never touches a database and the reader never sees a sidebar.', 'content' => '

What was built

  • Custom post types separating submissions from published pieces
  • Editorial status flow for the review queue
  • Front-end filters by form and theme

Myangustis is a live project focused on Burmese text processing on the web — the unglamorous fundamentals: Unicode correctness, font stacks that actually render, and input handling that does not fight the writer.

Why it matters

Most of my writing and translation work runs through Burmese text. Building the engine myself means the tooling matches the way the language is actually written.
